title: Respond to a new transfusion reaction
stem: During red-cell transfusion, a client develops new chills, fever and back discomfort. Which actions belong in the immediate reaction response? Select all that apply.
options: Discard the bag and tubing immediately.
Administer the prescribed antipyretic for the fever.
Stop the transfusion and promptly assess the client.
Notify the team and follow the reaction investigation protocol.
Slow the transfusion until the chills settle.
why: The component and set may be needed for investigation; follow the reaction protocol's handling instructions.
Symptom treatment may be ordered, but it must not displace stopping exposure and implementing the reaction response.
Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
Coordinated assessment, samples and product handling help establish the cause and guide treatment.
Reducing the rate still continues exposure to a component that may be causing a serious reaction.
takeaway: Further exposure should cease while the new systemic symptoms are assessed for a potentially serious reaction.
learningObjective: Initiate the transfusion-reaction pathway when new systemic symptoms develop during blood administration.

title: Differentiate possible transfusion overload
stem: An older client with heart failure develops breathlessness during transfusion. Which findings particularly support circulatory overload in the differential? Select all that apply.
options: Rising blood pressure with venous congestion.
Isolated urticaria with unchanged breathing and pressure.
Severe back pain with hypotension and dark urine.
New fever and rigors with clear lungs and stable pressure.
New crackles with increasing oxygen requirement.
why: The pressure and venous findings support increased circulatory volume during transfusion.
This pattern more strongly supports an allergic skin reaction than circulatory overload.
This pattern raises concern for hemolysis rather than isolated volume overload.
A febrile or other reaction needs urgent evaluation, but this pattern does not specifically support congestion.
Pulmonary congestion can impair oxygenation and supports overload in the differential.
takeaway: Pulmonary congestion can impair oxygenation and supports overload in the differential.
learningObjective: Recognize a circulatory-overload pattern during transfusion while arranging urgent assessment.

title: Report delayed transfusion symptoms
stem: A client is discharged after an uncomplicated transfusion. Which new findings should be reported promptly with mention of the recent transfusion? Select all that apply.
options: A small venipuncture bruise becomes lighter over several days.
New jaundice or unusually dark urine.
Unexpected fever, worsening fatigue or breathlessness.
Mild resolving tenderness where the cannula was removed.
Gradually improving tolerance of usual activities.
why: A resolving localized bruise is not the same pattern as new jaundice, dark urine or systemic illness.
Delayed hemolysis can become apparent after discharge; recent transfusion is important assessment information.
New systemic symptoms require prompt assessment and the transfusion history can guide investigation.
A improving local insertion-site symptom is less concerning than new systemic deterioration.
Functional improvement may reflect the intended benefit of red-cell treatment.
takeaway: Delayed hemolysis can become apparent after discharge; recent transfusion is important assessment information.
learningObjective: Include delayed warning symptoms in post-transfusion discharge teaching.

title: Resolve a blood-unit identity discrepancy
stem: A blood unit's compatibility label has an identification number that differs from the client's wristband by one digit. The name matches. What is appropriate?
options: Ask the client to confirm their blood group
Correct the number on the label at the bedside
Stop the verification process and resolve the discrepancy
Use the matching name to approve the unit
why: A remembered blood group cannot replace compatibility and identity checks.
A handwritten correction does not establish the blood bank's intended compatibility.
All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
A name match does not resolve a potentially serious identification error.
takeaway: All required identifiers must agree before exposing the client to the component.
learningObjective: Verify concordant client and component identifiers before transfusion.

title: Confirm compatible red-cell tubing fluid
stem: A red-cell unit is ready, but the intended line contains dextrose solution. What should the nurse do?
options: Connect the unit through the existing dextrose line.
Reduce the dextrose rate during transfusion.
Use the dextrose solution to prime the blood filter.
Establish an approved compatible blood-administration setup.
why: The dextrose solution's appearance does not establish compatibility with red cells.
A lower rate does not remove contact between the incompatible solution and blood.
Priming still leaves the solution in the pathway where it will contact the cells.
Red cells need a suitable fluid and tubing plan; normal saline is commonly used according to local policy.
takeaway: Red cells need a suitable fluid and tubing plan; normal saline is commonly used according to local policy.
learningObjective: Use approved compatibility guidance for fluids sharing red-cell administration tubing.

title: Assess a new fever before transfusion
stem: Immediately before a planned nonemergency transfusion, a client reports chills. Temperature is newly 38.4°C on two measurements; the nurse has assessed vital signs and current symptoms, and the unit is not connected. What is the best next action?
options: Report the changed baseline and clarify whether to start.
Obtain the routine pretransfusion premedication prescription.
Repeat the temperature once more after a rest period.
Collect cultures if they are part of the existing illness orders.
why: The new febrile illness needs review before transfusion and would complicate assessment of any subsequent reaction.
Premedication does not explain the current symptoms or establish that starting is appropriate.
The elevation has already been confirmed and assessed; further repetition should not replace communication of the change.
Cultures may be useful but do not resolve the decision about initiating the planned component in a changed clinical state.
takeaway: The new febrile illness needs review before transfusion and would complicate assessment of any subsequent reaction.
learningObjective: Establish and communicate a changed baseline before initiating a prescribed blood component.

title: Evaluate a platelet transfusion response
stem: A client with thrombocytopenia receives prescribed platelets for mucosal bleeding. Which observations most directly assess the intended hemostatic response? Select all that apply.
options: Less mucosal oozing and no additional bleeding sites.
An increased hemoglobin with better exertional tolerance.
A normal temperature with no chills during administration.
A stable weight and blood pressure after the infusion.
The platelet count measured at the ordered post-transfusion time.
why: Clinical hemostasis shows whether the intended bleeding problem is improving.
This cluster more directly evaluates correction of red-cell anemia than platelet response.
These are important safety findings but do not demonstrate hemostatic effectiveness.
These help assess fluid tolerance rather than the intended platelet-count and bleeding response.
An appropriately timed result helps assess the platelet increment.
takeaway: An appropriately timed result helps assess the platelet increment.
learningObjective: Use platelet and bleeding findings to evaluate platelet-component therapy.

title: Explain a prescribed plasma component
stem: A client with a documented clotting-factor deficiency is prescribed plasma and asks why red cells are not being used instead. What explanation is most accurate?
options: Plasma directly increases the circulating platelet count.
Plasma stimulates the bone marrow to produce replacement red cells.
Plasma supplies clotting factors for the identified deficiency.
Plasma raises oxygen-carrying capacity in the same way as red cells.
why: A platelet component, rather than plasma, supplies platelets when that is the indicated need.
Plasma supplies proteins; it is not an erythropoiesis-stimulating treatment.
The component is selected to replace the deficient coagulation proteins.
Oxygen transport is primarily a red-cell function, not the principal purpose of plasma here.
takeaway: The component is selected to replace the deficient coagulation proteins.
learningObjective: Distinguish clotting-factor replacement from red-cell or platelet replacement.

title: Manage an unexpected PN interruption
stem: A client's continuous high-dextrose parenteral nutrition stops unexpectedly because the line fails. Alternative access and the prescribed interruption plan are being arranged. Why is an early glucose check particularly relevant?
options: Glucose must immediately rise when any PN infusion is interrupted.
The lost protein supply causes a glucose decline before carbohydrate changes matter.
A normal glucose before the interruption predicts stability until the next bag.
Glucose may fall after the abrupt reduction in carbohydrate delivery.
why: Stopping the carbohydrate supply does not predict an immediate rise; the actual response must be measured.
The immediate interruption concern is the change in dextrose delivery rather than rapid depletion of body protein.
A previous reading cannot establish the response to an abrupt change in substrate delivery.
The metabolic response to continuous glucose delivery may persist after it stops; assessment guides the ordered contingency treatment.
takeaway: The metabolic response to continuous glucose delivery may persist after it stops; assessment guides the ordered contingency treatment.
learningObjective: Explain glucose monitoring after an abrupt interruption of continuous high-dextrose parenteral nutrition.

title: Monitor a new PN regimen
stem: During the first two days of PN in a malnourished client, which trends require prompt review? Select all that apply.
options: Glucose increases to 19 mmol/L above the prescribed target of 6–10.
Phosphate falls to 0.45 mmol/L (reference 0.80–1.45).
New fever accompanies redness and tenderness at the catheter site.
Weight rises 0.1 kg while pressure, lung sounds and balance remain stable.
The client remains alert with glucose within the prescribed target.
why: Significant hyperglycemia indicates a need to review metabolic tolerance and the authorized regimen.
The decline during refeeding can be clinically important and requires electrolyte and nutrition-plan review.
The combination raises concern for a vascular-access infection and needs prompt assessment.
This small isolated change does not itself establish fluid intolerance, although trends remain necessary.
These observations are reassuring at that time and do not represent the new problems being sought.
takeaway: Significant hyperglycemia indicates a need to review metabolic tolerance and the authorized regimen.
learningObjective: Select metabolic, fluid and access assessments after parenteral nutrition is initiated.

title: Verify central PN access requirements
stem: A PN bag is labelled for central administration, but only a peripheral cannula is currently usable. What is appropriate?
options: Dilute the bag at the bedside to make it peripheral
Clarify access or an alternative formulation before infusion
Use the peripheral cannula because it flushes easily
Run the central formulation slowly through the peripheral line
why: Unapproved dilution compromises formulation and compounding safety.
A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
Patency does not establish that the formulation is suitable for that vessel.
A slower rate does not necessarily make its concentration appropriate.
takeaway: A central formulation may be unsuitable for peripheral veins.
learningObjective: Match a central PN formulation to a verified appropriate vascular-access route.

title: Protect a dedicated PN lumen
stem: A client has a designated central-lumen PN infusion and another usable lumen. Which practices support safe delivery? Select all that apply.
options: Verify a proposed co-infusion with an approved compatibility resource.
Add an ordered IV medicine into the hanging PN bag.
Use the PN lumen for the next antibiotic while the other lumen remains available.
Join a medicine to PN after checking that both fluids are clear.
Continue PN through its designated lumen.
why: PN contains multiple ingredients, so compatibility requires specific confirmation.
Bedside addition is not an approved compounding method and can affect stability and dose delivery.
A separate suitable lumen avoids unnecessary PN interruption and mixing; access choice should follow the dedicated-lumen plan.
Some incompatibilities are not visible, so clarity cannot replace a compatibility determination.
Dedicated use limits unnecessary interruption and reduces opportunities for incompatible mixing.
takeaway: Dedicated use limits unnecessary interruption and reduces opportunities for incompatible mixing.
learningObjective: Limit incompatibility and unnecessary manipulation of the parenteral-nutrition pathway.

title: Recognize refeeding-associated electrolyte decline
stem: Within a day of restarting nutrition, a severely malnourished client develops weakness and phosphate falls from 1.0 to 0.32 mmol/L (reference 0.80–1.45). Kidney function is unchanged and there are no new gastrointestinal losses. Which mechanism is most concerning?
options: Reduced kidney excretion causing phosphate retention.
A newly inadequate ongoing dietary phosphate intake.
Simple dilution from a large-volume fluid bolus.
An intracellular electrolyte shift associated with refeeding.
why: Retention would tend to increase phosphate and does not fit the marked fall with unchanged renal function.
The abrupt decline after feeding starts is more suggestive of redistribution than a new reduction in intake.
No such exposure is described; the severe malnutrition and timing after nutrition support refeeding physiology.
Renewed carbohydrate metabolism can drive phosphate into cells; the abrupt fall and weakness require urgent review of electrolytes and nutrition progression.
takeaway: Renewed carbohydrate metabolism can drive phosphate into cells; the abrupt fall and weakness require urgent review of electrolytes and nutrition progression.
learningObjective: Escalate new phosphate depletion and weakness after nutrition is restarted in severe malnutrition.

title: Explain prescribed isotonic volume replacement
stem: A client with vomiting and circulatory volume depletion is prescribed an isotonic crystalloid. What is the principal immediate treatment goal?
options: Support extracellular volume and circulating perfusion.
Replace intracellular free water as its main purpose.
Expand plasma oncotic pressure through added protein.
Supply the glucose needed for immediate caloric replacement.
why: An isotonic crystalloid can restore extracellular volume when vomiting has reduced intravascular filling.
This is more characteristic of a hypotonic free-water strategy than isotonic volume resuscitation.
A crystalloid does not provide colloid protein for that purpose.
The stated isotonic volume goal does not establish a glucose-containing nutritional prescription.
takeaway: An isotonic crystalloid can restore extracellular volume when vomiting has reduced intravascular filling.
learningObjective: Connect an isotonic crystalloid prescription with treatment of extracellular volume depletion.

title: Monitor prescribed hypertonic saline
stem: A client receives hypertonic saline under a protocol that limits the sodium rise to 8 mmol/L in any 24 hours and requires serial neurological and sodium checks. Which findings require prompt action under that protocol? Select all that apply.
options: Sodium rises from 112 to 123 mmol/L within 10 hours.
New headache and declining alertness develop during infusion.
Sodium rises 2 mmol/L in four hours while alertness improves.
Blood pressure remains close to its pretreatment value.
The verified pump rate matches the current authorized order.
why: The 11 mmol/L rise already exceeds the supplied 24-hour limit and requires urgent review of correction safety.
A neurological change during correction requires immediate assessment rather than being assumed to reflect recovery.
This finding alone does not exceed the stated limit, though the full ongoing 24-hour trend must still be monitored.
A stable pressure is not a new warning finding and does not replace sodium and neurological checks.
A correct setting is necessary but does not eliminate the need to act on adverse clinical or laboratory trends.
takeaway: The 11 mmol/L rise already exceeds the supplied 24-hour limit and requires urgent review of correction safety.
learningObjective: Apply controlled-rate and neurological monitoring during authorized hypertonic saline treatment.

title: Assess urine output before potassium replacement
stem: An IV potassium replacement order requires urine output of at least 30 mL/hour before infusion. Potassium from two hours ago is 3.3 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0). Output has fallen to 10 mL/hour with rising creatinine, and the infusion has not started. What is the best action?
options: Use a more dilute preparation for the same dose.
Request a new potassium level and proceed with the current order meanwhile.
Hold initiation and clarify the replacement order.
Start the dose because the recent potassium remains low.
why: Dilution changes concentration but not the total potassium load or unmet start criterion.
A repeat may be needed, but administering during clarification would disregard the specified output parameter.
The new renal findings violate the supplied condition and may reduce potassium elimination, so the plan needs review.
The low value does not override the explicit urine-output condition or the new renal change.
takeaway: The new renal findings violate the supplied condition and may reduce potassium elimination, so the plan needs review.
learningObjective: Recognize reduced potassium elimination as relevant before a replacement infusion.

title: Recognize magnesium toxicity
stem: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has a respiratory rate of 8/minute, absent deep-tendon reflexes and falling urine output. Another nurse is activating emergency help and supporting breathing. What medication-related action should occur first under the toxicity protocol?
options: Draw the ordered magnesium blood sample.
Review the total magnesium received during the shift.
Prepare the prescribed calcium rescue medicine.
Stop the magnesium infusion.
why: A sample supports assessment but should not delay stopping the suspected toxic infusion.
Exposure history is useful for the team, but the current clinical toxicity requires an immediate infusion action.
Rescue preparation may be urgent, but continued magnesium exposure should be stopped as that treatment is arranged.
Stopping further exposure addresses the suspected toxicity while respiratory support and the rest of the emergency protocol proceed.
takeaway: Stopping further exposure addresses the suspected toxicity while respiratory support and the rest of the emergency protocol proceed.
learningObjective: Escalate respiratory depression and loss of reflexes during magnesium sulfate infusion.

title: Distinguish seizure prophylaxis from pressure control
stem: A client with severe preeclampsia receives magnesium sulfate and a separate antihypertensive. They ask why both are needed. What is best?
options: Magnesium reduces seizure risk; the other medicine treats hypertension.
Magnesium treats hypertension; the other medicine prevents seizures.
Magnesium removes retained fluid; the other medicine treats hypertension.
Magnesium relaxes the uterus; the other medicine prevents seizures.
why: The two prescriptions address distinct complications of severe preeclampsia.
This reverses their principal intended roles in the stated plan.
Magnesium is not prescribed here primarily as a diuretic.
These purposes do not explain the prescribed seizure-prevention and pressure-control regimen.
takeaway: The two prescriptions address distinct complications of severe preeclampsia.
learningObjective: Explain why magnesium and a separate antihypertensive may both be prescribed in severe preeclampsia.

title: Review a possibly contaminated heparin sample
stem: A heparin-monitoring sample drawn through the infusing lumen is unexpectedly very high. The nurse has reported the critical result and sampling route; the client has no new bleeding. The local protocol requires team guidance for a possibly contaminated result. What should follow?
options: Repeat the sample through the same infusing lumen.
Obtain interim protocol guidance and a fresh appropriate-site sample.
Apply the routine dose-reduction table to this value.
Verify the infusion pump and use its setting to accept the result.
why: Repeating the same collection problem may produce another contaminated result unless an appropriate validated sampling method is used.
The value might be genuinely high or contaminated; immediate guidance plus valid repeat testing avoids both dismissal and unverified dose changes.
Possible contamination changes interpretation, and the supplied protocol requires guidance before using the routine table.
Checking programming is useful but does not establish that the sample reflects systemic anticoagulation.
takeaway: The value might be genuinely high or contaminated; immediate guidance plus valid repeat testing avoids both dismissal and unverified dose changes.
learningObjective: Consider sampling contamination before interpreting an unexpected anticoagulation result.

title: Recognize an unexpectedly high neuraxial block
stem: During epidural analgesia, an alert client develops numbness extending into both hands, increasing limb heaviness, low blood pressure and difficulty taking a deep breath. Which complication is most concerning?
options: A vasovagal episode.
Hypovolemia from earlier fasting.
An unexpectedly high neuraxial block.
Opioid-related sedation.
why: A vagal response can lower pressure but does not explain the ascending bilateral numbness and motor heaviness.
Low volume can contribute to hypotension but does not explain the new level of sensory and motor blockade.
Ascending sensory and motor changes with respiratory and circulatory effects require immediate epidural-protocol response and anesthesia review.
The client is alert and has a spreading sensory-motor block, which is more specific than isolated opioid sedation.
takeaway: Ascending sensory and motor changes with respiratory and circulatory effects require immediate epidural-protocol response and anesthesia review.
learningObjective: Escalate spreading weakness and breathing difficulty during epidural analgesia.

title: Recognize systemic local-anesthetic toxicity
stem: During a local-anesthetic procedure, a client develops ringing ears, metallic taste and slurred speech. Which responses are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the client to practise slow breathing for procedural anxiety.
Offer a brief pause and then complete the remaining anesthetic dose.
Alert the procedural team and stop further anesthetic administration.
Prepare airway and circulatory support according to the emergency protocol.
Use the prescribed antiemetic to treat the metallic taste and nausea.
why: Anxiety support may help distress but is not an adequate response to these drug-related neurological warning symptoms.
Resuming exposure before the team resolves the suspected toxicity could worsen the event.
Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
Toxicity can progress to seizures and cardiac instability, so early resuscitation readiness matters.
Symptom treatment does not address the characteristic neurological toxicity pattern.
takeaway: Tinnitus, metallic taste and slurred speech can be early systemic toxicity; preventing further exposure is urgent.
learningObjective: Respond to early neurological warning symptoms during local-anesthetic administration.

title: Respond to an open central-line system
stem: A central-line connection opens and the client develops sudden dyspnea and chest discomfort. Which immediate physical action best interrupts the suspected mechanism while help is summoned?
options: Occlude the open central-line system.
Apply supplemental oxygen.
Measure blood pressure and oxygen saturation.
Reconnect the monitoring leads.
why: Sealing the open pathway prevents further air entry while emergency assessment and treatment proceed.
Oxygen is important supportive care but does not stop additional air entering through the open connection.
Measurements guide care but do not interrupt the source of possible air entry.
Monitoring may support assessment but does not stop the open-line mechanism.
takeaway: Sealing the open pathway prevents further air entry while emergency assessment and treatment proceed.
learningObjective: Stop further air entry and escalate sudden symptoms after central-line disconnection.

title: Account for medicine remaining in tubing
stem: A small-volume IV medicine has left the bag, but medication-containing fluid remains in the tubing. A compatible flush volume and rate are prescribed. What should the nurse do?
options: Increase the next dose to replace the estimated residual
Complete the prescribed flush at the specified rate
Disconnect immediately because the medication bag is empty
Flush rapidly to finish the medication round
why: Dose compensation is unprescribed and the residual should be managed now.
This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
An empty bag does not mean the full intended dose has reached the client.
Rapid flushing can deliver residual medicine faster than prescribed.
takeaway: This delivers the residual medicine without an unintended rapid bolus.
learningObjective: Use the prescribed compatible flush plan to deliver residual medicine safely after a small-volume infusion.

title: Maintain blood integrity when transfusion is delayed
stem: A nonemergency transfusion is postponed after the blood unit arrives on the unit. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep the unit at the bedside until the new start time is confirmed.
Put the unit in an ice-filled cooler from the ward.
Contact the blood bank and follow its return or storage instructions.
Place the unit in the ward medication refrigerator.
why: The period of uncontrolled storage matters even when the intended delay appears short.
Improvised cooling can expose the component to unvalidated temperatures and does not replace an approved storage process.
Blood integrity depends on validated time-temperature control; the service can guide safe handling of this delayed unit.
An ordinary medication refrigerator may not provide validated blood-storage conditions.
takeaway: Blood integrity depends on validated time-temperature control; the service can guide safe handling of this delayed unit.
learningObjective: Follow blood-bank time and storage requirements when an issued component cannot be started.

title: Limit injection-site bruising
stem: After a prescribed subcutaneous enoxaparin injection, the client sees a small drop of blood and begins rubbing the site. Which technique should the nurse reinforce?
options: Massage briefly to disperse the medicine under the skin.
Rub the site with an alcohol swab until the drop disappears.
Press and rub an adhesive dressing firmly over the site.
Hold gentle gauze pressure if needed and avoid rubbing.
why: Massage is not needed to disperse enoxaparin and can increase local trauma.
Repeated rubbing can worsen bruising and is not the appropriate way to control oozing.
A dressing may be used as indicated, but rubbing pressure is not the supported postinjection technique.
Gentle pressure can control minor oozing; rubbing adds tissue trauma and bruising risk.
takeaway: Gentle pressure can control minor oozing; rubbing adds tissue trauma and bruising risk.
learningObjective: Apply product-specific subcutaneous anticoagulant technique and avoid unnecessary tissue trauma.
